Discussion of Ordinance Amendments 2 WHITE LAKE TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION OCTOBER 15, 2026 Item A. Planning Consultants David and Mateo, together with Township Attorney Deb, presented a draft data center zoning ordinance for Commission review in advance of a public hearing. The following topics were discussed, with staff directed to refine the draft accordingly. No formal motions or votes were taken on the ordinance itself; this remains a discussion item pending a public hearing. Overlay District and Location The Commission expressed general support for establishing a dedicated Data Center Overlay District (approximately 230 acres across roughly 18-20 parcels) in the northeast corner of the Township near the existing Mack Industries site, rather than permitting data centers as a special land use throughout the entire LM (Light Manufacturing) district. The rationale discussed included consistency with the Master Plan's future land use designation for industrial expansion in that area and a desire to limit data center siting to a defined, already industrially-oriented area. Setbacks Consensus leaned toward retaining a 300-foot setback measured from the property line of the applicable structure or equipment to residentially-zoned property lines, with acknowledgment that this figure could be increased (e.g., to 500 feet) if warranted. The Commission discussed using the setback as a supporting measure for noise, emissions, and visual massing concerns rather than as a standalone requirement. Noise and Vibration The draft ordinance's noise standards (45 dB residential standard, with a 6-decibel tonal penalty), vibration provisions, and infrasound concerns were discussed at length. The Commission was provided redlined additions from a sound and vibration consultant engaged by a neighboring township (Lion Township) for consideration prior to the public hearing. Staff noted that three acoustical consulting firms had been contacted; one indicated a baseline noise study would be required (at a cost of approximately 20,000 dollars) and declined to comment further, while responses from the other two were pending. Water Use and Natural Resources The draft ordinance's groundwater and surface water provisions (baseline groundwater assessment, monitoring, and contingency/mitigation plans) were reviewed. Discussion included whether to require closed-loop cooling systems rather than evaporative systems; several Commission members expressed support for requiring closed-loop systems, though no formal decision was made. It was clarified that water withdrawal and discharge approvals generally fall under the jurisdiction of Oakland County Health Department or the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), not the Township. Decommissioning The draft ordinance's decommissioning financial guarantee (currently set at 125% of estimated cost, reviewed and adjusted every 5 years for inflation) was discussed. A recommendation was made to increase the guarantee to 150%, consistent with standard practice referenced by a Commission member with real estate experience. Discussion also addressed clarifying that the Township select (rather than merely approve) the qualified professional preparing the decommissioning cost estimate, and that the Township retain the right to challenge the estimate. 3 WHITE LAKE TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION OCTOBER 15, 2026 Item A. Enforcement and Remedies The Commission discussed adding express authority for the Township to initiate legal proceedings to obtain compliance, in addition to existing remedies, within the operational compliance/escrow section of the ordinance. The Township Attorney indicated this language had been intended for inclusion and would be confirmed/added. Annual Reporting and Generators The Commission discussed whether annual third-party inspection/reporting requirements (and the associated funding escrow) should be specific to data centers or extended more broadly to any use exceeding a defined threshold of generators or electrical wattage, in order to avoid the appearance of singling out data centers. Consensus was to explore a broader, metric-based threshold (by generator count and/or wattage) for potential inclusion in the LM district standards or nuisance ordinance. Transfer of Ownership A Commission member raised concern that the draft's transfer-of-ownership provisions were vague regarding successor obligations. The Township Attorney agreed to review and clarify this section. Architectural Standards The draft ordinance's architectural review requirements for data center structures were discussed; no changes were proposed, though members noted the inconsistency with the lack of similar requirements for other LM district uses. Appeal Procedure It was clarified that provisions within the draft ordinance (including the operational compliance escrow section) would be appealable to the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA), consistent with other zoning ordinance provisions. Moratorium and Timeline Staff noted the Township's data center moratorium expires February 12, 2027, and has previously been extended once. The Commission discussed the possibility of deferring final action to a second November meeting, if needed, to allow additional review time while still meeting the moratorium deadline. Ambient Sound Level: The all-encompassing sound level associated with a given environment at a specified location and time, typically a composite of sound from many sources, near and far. Background Sound Level: The sound level that is present in a given environment at a specified location and time, in the absence of any identified intermittent or intrusive sound sources, typically characterized by the sound level exceeded 90 percent of the measurement period (L90). Battery Energy Storage System (BESS): One or more devices, assemblies, or containers capable of storing electrical energy for later use through electrochemical technologies, including associated control systems, inverters, transformers, cooling systems, fire-suppression equipment, and related infrastructure. C-Weighted Sound Level (dBC): The sound pressure level, expressed in decibels (dB), as measured using the C-weighting frequency network of a sound level meter conforming to American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard S1.4 for sound level meters. C-weighting applies little or no adjustment across most of the audible frequency spectrum, and includes lowfrequency energy typically down to 10 or 12.5 Hz, below the normally recognized range of human hearing.
